Short answer: it’s mostly confounding and measurement error. In cross‑sectional NHANES, absolute intakes of any nutrient are strong proxies for “how much food” people eat. People who eat more (typically younger, larger, often male) also tend to have higher diastolic BP. If you relate unadjusted absolute sodium, potassium, or magnesium to DBP, they will all look positively associated—masking potassium’s and magnesium’s true BP‑lowering effects seen in trials where energy and co‑nutrients are controlled.

What drives the paradox
- Energy intake confounding: Absolute Na, K, and Mg scale with total calories. Calorie intake correlates with body size and DBP. Without proper energy adjustment (residual or nutrient‑density models), every nutrient tends to “inherit” the calorie–BP relation.
- Body size/adiposity confounding: Bigger people eat more and have higher BP. If body size and adiposity aren’t modeled carefully (and sometimes nonlinearly), residual confounding remains.
- Age/sex confounding and DBP’s shape: DBP peaks in midlife and declines in older age; older adults also eat fewer calories. Insufficiently flexible adjustment for age/sex can yield spurious positive associations.
- Cross‑sectional design and reverse causation/collider bias: Diagnosed hypertensives may change diet (lower Na, raise K/Mg) and take medications (especially diuretics that affect K/Mg). Conditioning on diagnosis or medications can induce collider bias; mixing treated and untreated can blur true relations.
- Dietary measurement error and under‑reporting: 24‑hour recalls are noisy; under‑reporting correlates with BMI and health status. Errors are strongly tied to energy intake, biasing nutrient–BP associations.
- Co‑linearity among minerals: Na, K, and Mg intakes are correlated; mutual adjustment without clear design can produce unstable or counterintuitive coefficients.
- Acute vs chronic biology: A single day’s intake poorly captures longer‑term mineral status relevant to BP regulation.

How to make NHANES line up better with RCT evidence
- Use energy‑adjusted exposures:
  - Residual model (regress nutrient on total kcal; use residuals).
  - Nutrient density (e.g., mg per 1000 kcal).
  - Consider Na:K ratio (robust predictor of BP).
- Adjust carefully for confounders:
  - Flexible age splines; sex; race/ethnicity; BMI/waist (and consider whether adiposity is a mediator vs confounder for your causal question); alcohol; physical activity; smoking; SES.
- Handle treatment and diagnosis:
  - Prefer analyses in untreated participants, or apply validated corrections for antihypertensive therapy (e.g., add 5 mmHg to DBP for treated, or use censored normal/Heckman models), and avoid conditioning on colliders.
- Improve exposure measurement:
  - Use both NHANES 24‑hr recall days with NCI usual‑intake methods.
  - Calibrate intakes using biomarker studies where possible; when available, prefer 24‑hr urinary Na and K (or at least Na:K from spot urine, recognizing formula biases).
  - Sensitivity analyses limited to plausible energy reporters (e.g., Goldberg cutoffs).
- Model nonlinearity and interactions:
  - Check for nonlinearity in nutrient–BP relations and effect modification by age, sex, adiposity, and sodium intake (salt sensitivity).
- Don’t put all three minerals in the same naive model; consider substitution/partitioning frameworks that reflect realistic dietary tradeoffs.

Take‑home: The positive cross‑sectional associations of K and Mg with DBP in NHANES are artifacts of absolute intake modeling, confounding (especially by calories, body size, age/sex), and measurement/treatment issues. Once you use energy‑adjusted nutrient measures, avoid collider bias from treatment/diagnosis, and reduce measurement error, observational results tend to align with trials: higher potassium (and likely magnesium) density associates with lower BP, and higher sodium (or higher Na:K) associates with higher BP.
